narrative:
The model predicted a 71.7% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile is far below the average of accepted students, who typically rank near the middle of their class. Your first-year ranking had the next largest impact and also pulled the outcome toward failure; again, a bottom-decile position contrasts sharply with the much stronger average performance of admitted applicants.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 2.70 it is below the 3.23 average of accepted students, yet the model still saw this value as a modest positive signal that slightly increased the chance you might pass. Unfortunately, this encouraging nudge was not nearly enough to offset the much larger negative effects from your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 29, family income in the middle bracket, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time played little or no role in the final decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and class standing in law school. Stronger grades and higher rankings in future years can substantially lower your predicted risk of failing the bar. Consider academic support programs, study skills coaching, or a structured bar-preparation course once you are enrolled.
